prime.problem: When nothing appears on screen, you can't tell whether the request is crossing the network, waiting for a free chip, loading weights, reading your prompt or thinking. Each has a different fix, and the spread is huge: 0.13 s to over two minutes.
prime.fits: The first metric card. The overview split a response into a start and a writing time; this card opens up the start. Output speed and output length, next, cover the writing time.
prime.goal: Given a setup, name which part of the time to first token dominates and which change would cut it.

attend: Which of the five parts can be zero in one setup and many seconds in another, and what flips each one?
Why does a 2,605-token prompt take 12.6 s to read on the M3 but a 10k-token prompt fits inside Baseten's 0.28 s?
Why does Sonnet 5's TTFT jump from 1.39 s to 141 s, and is that the same metric in both cases?
When is TTFT the wrong number to optimise even though users complain the app feels slow?

must: Everything before the first token happens in sequence → TTFT = network + queue + cold start + prefill (+ hidden thinking) → the largest part dominates → fix that one, not the sum

Prefill reads the whole prompt in one parallel pass → time grows with prompt length and chip speed → long prompts on a laptop take seconds, on a datacenter GPU a fraction of one → a cached prefix skips it
Reasoning models write hidden thinking before the first visible token → TTFT as reported can include minutes of output → separate "first token" from "first answer token"
elevated: Cold start copies the weights from disk → 4.07 s for the 3 GB model on the M3 → only when the model was unloaded, so keep_alive decides whether you ever see it
reference: TCP/TLS handshake details (53–77 ms round trip, 110–160 ms with handshake)
per-host TTFT values (Baseten 0.28 s, CoreWeave 1.35 s)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw TTFT as a bar of five segments in order. Label each with what causes it, what makes it zero, and the biggest value you saw on the card. Then write one sentence on when TTFT is the wrong metric.
checklist: network (≈ 0 locally, tens of ms hosted), queue (busy servers), cold start (only if unloaded), prefill (grows with prompt), hidden thinking (reasoning models)
cold start and thinking can be huge or zero depending on setup
prefill is skipped for a cached prefix
TTFT matters when a person watches a stream; for long or non-streamed answers, writing time dominates

retrieve.q: Explain why a provider can have the lowest TTFT but only middling output speed, in terms of what each metric measures.
answer: TTFT covers everything before the first token (network, queue, prefill)
output speed covers only tokens after the first
they depend on different things: prefill hardware and queue vs decode bandwidth and batching (Baseten: 0.28 s TTFT, 5th in speed)

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens between sending a request to Ollama on a cold M3 and the first token appearing. Which step takes most of the 4.3 s?
answer: weights (3 GB) are loaded from disk into memory: 4.07 s
the prompt is read (prefill): about 0.24 s
then the first token is written

retrieve.q: A background summarising job with stream:false takes 40 s per document. Someone proposes a host with half the TTFT. Is that worth it, and what would you measure first?
answer: probably not: with no streaming only end-to-end time matters
measure how much of the 40 s is TTFT vs writing time
if writing dominates, cut output length or pick a faster-per-token host instead

compare.q: TTFT and output speed are both "how fast". What does each one exclude on purpose, and which one decides the wait for a 20-token reply vs a 2,000-token reply?
answer: TTFT excludes writing time; output speed starts its clock at the first token
the split lets each metric show one cause
20 tokens: TTFT dominates; 2,000 tokens: output speed dominates

compare.q: The prefill part of TTFT and the per-token writing time run the same model on the same Mac. Why is reading a prompt token so much cheaper than writing an output token?
answer: prefill processes all prompt tokens in one parallel pass
each weight read is reused across many tokens, so it is compute-bound
decode reads every weight for one token at a time, so it is memory-bound (≈ 207 vs 15.4 t/s here)

predict.q: You double the prompt from 2,605 to about 5,200 tokens on the warm M3. Predict whether prefill time roughly doubles, more than doubles, or less, and give one reason it might not be exactly 2×.
predict.answer: Roughly doubles (about 25 s at 207 t/s), and a bit more in practice: attention work per token grows with the context already read, so later prompt tokens cost slightly more. The machine's load also swings it (12.6 vs 33.9 s for the same prompt). Caching the first 2,605 tokens would leave only the new half to read.

apply.task: Measure your own TTFT breakdown. With Ollama, run the same short prompt three ways: right after ollama stop (cold), again immediately (warm), and with a prompt about 10× longer. Read load_duration and prompt_eval_duration from /api/generate. For a hosted API, time the first streamed chunk for the same short and long prompts.
apply.done: You have a table with cold, warm and long-prompt rows showing which part dominates each, and you can say which fix (keep_alive, caching, shorter prompt) targets each row.
apply.hint: Durations in the Ollama response are in nanoseconds; divide by 1e9.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how prefill time scales with prompt length?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why a quoted TTFT for a reasoning model can be minutes long?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: prompt length → prefill time, or prefill → why caching helps?
In your own apps, is TTFT or writing time the part users actually notice?
What will you check first on the output-speed card?
